claim: A small fraction of HIV-1-infected humans develop broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) against HIV-1.
source: A small fraction of HIV-1- infected humans develop broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) against HIV-1 that protect macaques from simian immunodeficiency HIV chimeric virus (SHIV).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the HIV research field, supported by extensive literature.

claim: Human bNAbs protect macaques from simian immunodeficiency HIV chimeric virus (SHIV).
source: A small fraction of HIV-1- infected humans develop broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) against HIV-1 that protect macaques from simian immunodeficiency HIV chimeric virus (SHIV).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: A small number of macaques infected with SHIVs develop broadly neutralizing serologic activity.
source: Similarly, a small number of macaques infected with SHIVs develop broadly neutralizing serologic activity, but less is known about the nature of simian antibodies.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the abstract and supported by the study context.

claim: Ab1485 was isolated from a macaque infected with SHIVAD8 that developed broadly neutralizing serologic activity targeting the V3-glycan region of HIV-1 Env.
source: Here, we report on a monoclonal antibody, Ab1485, isolated from a macaque infected with SHIVAD8 that developed broadly neutralizing serologic activity targeting the V3-glycan region of HIV-1 Env.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ab1485 neutralizes 38.1% of HIV-1 isolates in a 42-pseudovirus panel with a geometric mean IC50 of 0.055 µg/mL.
source: Ab1485 neutralizes 38.1% of HIV-1 isolates in a 42-pseudovirus panel with a geometric mean IC50 of 0.055 µg/mLl and SHIVAD8 with an IC50 of 0.028 µg/mLl.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ab1485 neutralizes SHIVAD8 with an IC50 of 0.028 µg/mL.
source: Ab1485 neutralizes 38.1% of HIV-1 isolates in a 42-pseudovirus panel with a geometric mean IC50 of 0.055 µg/mLl and SHIVAD8 with an IC50 of 0.028 µg/mLl.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ab1485 binds the V3-glycan epitope in a glycan-dependent manner.
source: Ab1485 binds the V3-glycan epitope in a glycan-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assays with glycan mutants shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A 3.5 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of Ab1485 in complex with a native-like SOSIP Env trimer showed conserved contacts with the N332gp120 glycan and gp120 GDIR peptide motif.
source: A 3.5 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of Ab1485 in complex with a native-like SOSIP Env trimer showed conserved contacts with the N332gp120 glycan and gp120 GDIR peptide motif, but in a distinct Env-binding orientation relative to human V3/N332gp120 glycan-targeting bNAbs.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Ab1485 binds Env in a distinct orientation relative to human V3/N332gp120 glycan-targeting bNAbs.
source: A 3.5 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of Ab1485 in complex with a native-like SOSIP Env trimer showed conserved contacts with the N332gp120 glycan and gp120 GDIR peptide motif, but in a distinct Env-binding orientation relative to human V3/N332gp120 glycan-targeting bNAbs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparisons shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Intravenous infusion of Ab1485 protected macaques from a high dose challenge with SHIVAD8.
source: Intravenous infusion of Ab1485 protected macaques from a high dose challenge with SHIVAD8.
evidence: This is supported by the protection data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Macaques can develop bNAbs against the V3-glycan patch that resemble human V3-glycan bNAbs.
source: We conclude that macaques can develop bNAbs against the V3-glycan patch that resemble human V3-glycan bNAbs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined structural and functional data.

claim: bNAbs target several different conserved epitopes on the HIV-1 Envelope spike protein (Env) using multiple mechanisms of binding.
source: Over the last decade, characterization of monoclonal antibodies isolated from HIV-1-infected individuals with broad and potent serologic activity against the virus, revealed that bNAbs target several different conserved epitopes on the HIV-1 Envelope spike protein (Env) using multiple mechanisms of binding (Burton and Hangartner, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burton and Hangartner, 2016.

claim: The target epitopes of many bNAbs combine host-derived glycans with protein components of Env.
source: The target epitopes of many bNAbs are unusual because they combine host-derived glycans with protein components of Env.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: bNAb maturation is mediated by somatic hypermutation.
source: Longitudinal cohort and structural studies demonstrated that bNAb maturation mediated by somatic hypermutation (Wei et al., 2003; Liao et al., 2013; Bonsignori et al., 2017; Bonsignori et al., 2016; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2012; Bhiman et al., 2015) occurs in part to accommodate the host-derived glycans that shield Env (Wei et al., 2003; Liao et al., 2013; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2012; Bhiman et al., 2015; Kong et al., 2013; Garces et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to longitudinal studies.

claim: bNAb maturation occurs in part to accommodate the host-derived glycans that shield Env.
source: Longitudinal cohort and structural studies demonstrated that bNAb maturation mediated by somatic hypermutation (Wei et al., 2003; Liao et al., 2013; Bonsignori et al., 2017; Bonsignori et al., 2016; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2012; Bhiman et al., 2015) occurs in part to accommodate the host-derived glycans that shield Env (Wei et al., 2003; Liao et al., 2013; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2012; Bhiman et al., 2015; Kong et al., 2013; Garces et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The V3-glycan supersite is an oligomannose patch around the V3 base of Env and the potential N-linked glycosylation site at position 332 of the Env gp120 subunit.
source: One of these epitopes, is the V3-glycan supersite, an oligomannose patch around the V3 base of Env and the potential N-linked glycosylation site at position 332 of the Env gp120 subunit (Kong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kong et al., 2013.

claim: bNAbs to the V3-glycan site are among the most potent anti HIV-1 antibodies isolated to date.
source: bNAbs to this site are among the most potent anti HIV-1 antibodies isolated to date and have considerable breadth, moreover, they are among the most frequently elicited upon natural infection with HIV-1 in humans (Walker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2010.

claim: V3-glycan bNAbs have considerable breadth.
source: bNAbs to this site are among the most potent anti HIV-1 antibodies isolated to date and have considerable breadth, moreover, they are among the most frequently elicited upon natural infection with HIV-1 in humans (Walker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2010.

claim: V3-glycan bNAbs are among the most frequently elicited upon natural infection with HIV-1 in humans.
source: bNAbs to this site are among the most potent anti HIV-1 antibodies isolated to date and have considerable breadth, moreover, they are among the most frequently elicited upon natural infection with HIV-1 in humans (Walker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2010.

claim: The family of V3-glycan bNAbs is highly diverse.
source: A number of structural studies have shown that the family of V3-glycan bNAbs is highly diverse.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by structural studies.

claim: V3-glycan bNAbs target the GDIR motif of Env using multiple angles of approach.
source: They target the GDIR motif of Env using multiple angles of approach and therefore accommodate different surrounding glycans (Kong et al., 2013; Mouquet et al., 2012; Walker et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: V3-glycan bNAbs accommodate different surrounding glycans.
source: They target the GDIR motif of Env using multiple angles of approach and therefore accommodate different surrounding glycans (Kong et al., 2013; Mouquet et al., 2012; Walker et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: V3-glycan bNAbs use a diverse group of heavy and light chain immunoglobulin genes.
source: V3-glycan bNAbs use a diverse group of heavy and light chain immunoglobulin genes and only some require the trimeric form of Env for binding (Longo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Longo et al., 2016.

claim: Only some V3-glycan bNAbs require the trimeric form of Env for binding.
source: V3-glycan bNAbs use a diverse group of heavy and light chain immunoglobulin genes and only some require the trimeric form of Env for binding (Longo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Longo et al., 2016.

claim: BG18 lacks some of the rare features observed in other potent bNAbs, such as insertions or deletions.
source: BNAbs to this site such as BG18 lack some of the rare features observed in other potent bNAbs, for instance the presence of insertions or deletions that are difficult to induce by vaccination (Freund et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Freund et al., 2017.

claim: The V3-glycan supersite is a good candidate epitope for anti HIV-1 vaccine design purposes.
source: Therefore, the V3-glycan supersite is a good candidate epitope for anti HIV-1 vaccine design purposes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of V3-glycan bNAbs described in the preceding text.

claim: bNAbs arise during natural infection in humans.
source: The observation that bNAbs arise during natural infection in humans (Binley et al., 2008; Doria-Rose et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Sather et al., 2009; Simek et al., 2009; Gray et al., 2011; Hraber et al., 2014; Rusert et al., 2016), and that they can block SHIV infection in macaques (Eichberg et al., 1992; Emini et al., 1992; Mascola et al., 1999; Mascola et al., 2000; Shibata et al., 1999; Baba et al., 2000; Parren et al., 2001; Hessell et al., 2009a; Hessell et al., 2009b; Hessell et al., 2010; Moldt et al., 2012), suggests that a vaccine that elicits such antibodies would be protective.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: bNAbs can block SHIV infection in macaques.
source: The observation that bNAbs arise during natural infection in humans (Binley et al., 2008; Doria-Rose et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Sather et al., 2009; Simek et al., 2009; Gray et al., 2011; Hraber et al., 2014; Rusert et al., 2016), and that they can block SHIV infection in macaques (Eichberg et al., 1992; Emini et al., 1992; Mascola et al., 1999; Mascola et al., 2000; Shibata et al., 1999; Baba et al., 2000; Parren et al., 2001; Hessell et al., 2009a; Hessell et al., 2009b; Hessell et al., 2010; Moldt et al., 2012), suggests that a vaccine that elicits such antibodies would be protective.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A vaccine that elicits bNAbs would be protective.
source: The observation that bNAbs arise during natural infection in humans (Binley et al., 2008; Doria-Rose et al., 2009; Li et al., 2009; Sather et al., 2009; Simek et al., 2009; Gray et al., 2011; Hraber et al., 2014; Rusert et al., 2016), and that they can block SHIV infection in macaques (Eichberg et al., 1992; Emini et al., 1992; Mascola et al., 1999; Mascola et al., 2000; Shibata et al., 1999; Baba et al., 2000; Parren et al., 2001; Hessell et al., 2009a; Hessell et al., 2009b; Hessell et al., 2010; Moldt et al., 2012), suggests that a vaccine that elicits such antibodies would be protective.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the cited evidence.

claim: All efforts to induce anti HIV-1 bNAbs by vaccination have produced only sporadic or less than optimal antibody responses with little or no protective activity against heterologous viral strains.
source: However, with the exception of experiments performed in genetically engineered mice (Dosenovic et al., 2015; Escolano et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2019), all efforts to induce anti HIV-1 bNAbs by vaccination have produced only sporadic or less than optimal antibody responses with little or no protective activity against heterologous viral strains (Xu et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2018 and Saunders et al., 2017.

claim: Experiments in genetically engineered mice have successfully induced anti HIV-1 bNAbs.
source: However, with the exception of experiments performed in genetically engineered mice (Dosenovic et al., 2015; Escolano et al., 2016; Saunders et al., 2019), all efforts to induce anti HIV-1 bNAbs by vaccination have produced only sporadic or less than optimal antibody responses with little or no protective activity against heterologous viral strains (Xu et al., 2018; Saunders et al., 2017).
evidence: This is implied by the exception clause and supported by citations.

claim: It remains unclear which animal model is most relevant to test candidate vaccines.
source: More importantly, it remains unclear which animal model is most relevant to test candidate vaccines.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Macaque CD4+ T cells are resistant to HIV-1.
source: Because macaque CD4+ T cells are resistant to HIV-1, SIV/HIV chimeric viruses (SHIVs), carrying the HIV-1 Env, were constructed to target and replicate efficiently in monkey CD4+ T lymphocytes in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: SIV/HIV chimeric viruses (SHIVs) carrying the HIV-1 Env were constructed to target and replicate efficiently in monkey CD4+ T lymphocytes in vivo.
source: Because macaque CD4+ T cells are resistant to HIV-1, SIV/HIV chimeric viruses (SHIVs), carrying the HIV-1 Env, were constructed to target and replicate efficiently in monkey CD4+ T lymphocytes in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most currently available SHIV challenge viruses do not possess replicative vigor and genetic variability and are unable to resist immunologic or cART pressure.
source: Unfortunately, most currently available SHIV challenge viruses do not possess this phenotype and are unable to resist immunologic or cART pressure.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of most SHIV models.

claim: SHIVAD8-EO is R5 tropic.
source: In contrast, molecularly cloned SHIVAD8-EO possesses many of the properties intrinsic to HIV-1. It is R5 tropic, produces sustained levels of plasma viremia in inoculated macaques, exhibits a Tier two neutralization sensitivity phenotype, generates resistant variants in bNAb and ART-treated animals, and causes irreversible depletions of CD4+ T cells in infected monkeys (Shingai et al., 2013; Gautam et al., 2012; Nishimura et al., 2010; Shingai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SHIVAD8-EO produces sustained levels of plasma viremia in inoculated macaques.
source: In contrast, molecularly cloned SHIVAD8-EO possesses many of the properties intrinsic to HIV-1. It is R5 tropic, produces sustained levels of plasma viremia in inoculated macaques, exhibits a Tier two neutralization sensitivity phenotype, generates resistant variants in bNAb and ART-treated animals, and causes irreversible depletions of CD4+ T cells in infected monkeys (Shingai et al., 2013; Gautam et al., 2012; Nishimura et al., 2010; Shingai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SHIVAD8-EO exhibits a Tier two neutralization sensitivity phenotype.
source: In contrast, molecularly cloned SHIVAD8-EO possesses many of the properties intrinsic to HIV-1. It is R5 tropic, produces sustained levels of plasma viremia in inoculated macaques, exhibits a Tier two neutralization sensitivity phenotype, generates resistant variants in bNAb and ART-treated animals, and causes irreversible depletions of CD4+ T cells in infected monkeys (Shingai et al., 2013; Gautam et al., 2012; Nishimura et al., 2010; Shingai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SHIVAD8-EO generates resistant variants in bNAb and ART-treated animals.
source: In contrast, molecularly cloned SHIVAD8-EO possesses many of the properties intrinsic to HIV-1. It is R5 tropic, produces sustained levels of plasma viremia in inoculated macaques, exhibits a Tier two neutralization sensitivity phenotype, generates resistant variants in bNAb and ART-treated animals, and causes irreversible depletions of CD4+ T cells in infected monkeys (Shingai et al., 2013; Gautam et al., 2012; Nishimura et al., 2010; Shingai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SHIVAD8-EO causes irreversible depletions of CD4+ T cells in infected monkeys.
source: In contrast, molecularly cloned SHIVAD8-EO possesses many of the properties intrinsic to HIV-1. It is R5 tropic, produces sustained levels of plasma viremia in inoculated macaques, exhibits a Tier two neutralization sensitivity phenotype, generates resistant variants in bNAb and ART-treated animals, and causes irreversible depletions of CD4+ T cells in infected monkeys (Shingai et al., 2013; Gautam et al., 2012; Nishimura et al., 2010; Shingai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: SHIVAD8-EO inoculation of macaques invariably leads to symptomatic immunodeficiency associated with opportunistic infections and a fatal clinical outcome in untreated animals.
source: SHIVAD8-EO inoculation of macaques invariably leads to symptomatic immunodeficiency associated with opportunistic infections and a fatal clinical outcome in untreated animals.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the SHIVAD8-EO model.

claim: A few SHIVAD8-EO-infected monkeys develop neutralizing antibodies against some heterologous clade A, B, and C HIV-1 strains.
source: As is the case for some HIV-1 infected individuals, a few SHIVAD8-EO-infected monkeys develop neutralizing antibodies against some heterologous clade A, B, and C HIV-1 strains (Walker et al., 2011b), including one macaque (CE8J) that exhibited the phenotype observed for HIV-1-infected human elite neutralizers (Walker et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2011b.

claim: Macaque CE8J exhibited the phenotype observed for HIV-1-infected human elite neutralizers.
source: As is the case for some HIV-1 infected individuals, a few SHIVAD8-EO-infected monkeys develop neutralizing antibodies against some heterologous clade A, B, and C HIV-1 strains (Walker et al., 2011b), including one macaque (CE8J) that exhibited the phenotype observed for HIV-1-infected human elite neutralizers (Walker et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2011b.

claim: The capacity to generate broadly neutralizing activity persisted throughout the 2 year infection of animal CE8J.
source: The capacity to generate broadly neutralizing activity persisted throughout the 2 year infection of animal CE8J.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about macaque CE8J.

claim: Macaque CE8J succumbed to immunodeficiency and was euthanized 117 weeks post-infection.
source: This monkey ultimately succumbed to immunodeficiency, and was euthanized 117 weeks post-infection.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the animal's outcome.

claim: Plasma mapping studies revealed that neutralizing activity of CE8J macaque exclusively targeted the glycan patch associated with the variable 3 (V3) loop on HIV-1 Env.
source: Plasma mapping studies revealed that neutralizing activity of CE8J macaque exclusively targeted the glycan patch associated with the variable 3 (V3) loop on HIV-1 Env, which is in agreement with studies of emerging viral variants in this macaque that presented substitutions of critical amino acids in the V3 region (Sadjadpour et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sadjadpour et al., 2013.

claim: Emerging viral variants in macaque CE8J presented substitutions of critical amino acids in the V3 region.
source: Plasma mapping studies revealed that neutralizing activity of CE8J macaque exclusively targeted the glycan patch associated with the variable 3 (V3) loop on HIV-1 Env, which is in agreement with studies of emerging viral variants in this macaque that presented substitutions of critical amino acids in the V3 region (Sadjadpour et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sadjadpour et al., 2013.

claim: Germinal center (GC) B cells that bound to YU2 gp140 fold-on trimer and BG505 SOSIP.664 trimer, but not to a control antigen, were purified from lymph nodes collected at the time of necropsy, 115 weeks post-SHIVAD8 infection.
source: To isolate bNAbs from macaque CE8J, we purified germinal center (GC) B cells that bound to YU2 gp140 fold-on trimer (YU2) and BG505 SOSIP.664 trimer (BG505), but not to a control antigen, from lymph nodes collected at the time of necropsy, 115 weeks post-SHIVAD8 infection (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the FACS data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Paired IgH and IgL/IgK sequences were obtained for 90 antibodies.
source: Paired IgH and IgL/IgK sequences were obtained for 90 antibodies.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the antibody cloning procedure.

claim: Among the 90 antibodies, two expanded B cell clones were found.
source: Among the 90 antibodies, we found two expanded B cell clones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IgH, IgL and IgK genes were somatically hypermutated with averages of 11.8, 8.5, and 4.1 average nucleotide mutations, respectively.
source: Sequence analysis revealed that IgH, IgL and IgK genes were somatically hypermutated (averages of 11.8, 8.5, and 4.1 average nucleotide mutations, respectively) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The average length of the complementarity determining region 3 of the heavy chain (CDRH3) was 15.3 amino acids.
source: The average length of the complementarity determining region 3 of the heavy chain (CDRH3) was 15.3 amino acids, and 30 of the antibodies had CDRH3s of 18 or more amino acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 30 of the antibodies had CDRH3s of 18 or more amino acids.
source: The average length of the complementarity determining region 3 of the heavy chain (CDRH3) was 15.3 amino acids, and 30 of the antibodies had CDRH3s of 18 or more amino acids (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 67 of the 90 monoclonal antibodies were produced.
source: We produced 67 of the 90 monoclonal antibodies and tested them for binding in ELISA to BG505, one of the Env baits that we used to isolate Env-binding B cells.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological step.

claim: Several antibodies showed detectable binding to BG505.
source: Several antibodies showed detectable binding to BG505, with Ab1485 showing the highest-level binding (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ab1485 showed the highest-level binding to BG505.
source: Several antibodies showed detectable binding to BG505, with Ab1485 showing the highest-level binding (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BG505.664 has been reported to bind to human bNAbs and show reduced binding to non-neutralizing antibodies.
source: BG505.664 has previously been reported to bind to human bNAbs and show reduced binding to non-neutralizing antibodies (Sanders et al., 2013), thus the three best binders to BG505 were evaluated for neutralizing activity in TZM-bl assays (Montefiori, 2005) against a screening panel of 7 HIV-1 pseudoviruses.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sanders et al., 2013.

claim: Only Ab1485 showed potent and broad activity against a screening panel of 7 HIV-1 pseudoviruses.
source: Only Ab1485 showed potent and broad activity against this panel (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) that could explain the activity previously detected in the plasma of macaque CE8J (Walker et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Ab1485 activity could explain the activity previously detected in the plasma of macaque CE8J.
source: Only Ab1485 showed potent and broad activity against this panel (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) that could explain the activity previously detected in the plasma of macaque CE8J (Walker et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the neutralization data and supported by citation.

claim: Ab1485 showed broader activity against the 42-virus panel than the human V3-glycan bNAb PGT135.
source: Ab1485 showed broader activity against this panel of pseudoviruses than the human V3-glycan bNAb PGT135, which neutralizes seven isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.14 µg/mL, but lower breadth than 10–1074 (25 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.16 µg/mL), PGT121 (23 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.1 µg/mL), 354BG18 (19 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.06 µg/mL) and PGT128 (22 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.04 µg/mL).
evidence: This is based on comparison of neutralization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Ab1485 showed lower breadth than 10–1074, PGT121, 354BG18 and PGT128.
source: Ab1485 showed broader activity against this panel of pseudoviruses than the human V3-glycan bNAb PGT135, which neutralizes seven isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.14 µg/mL, but lower breadth than 10–1074 (25 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.16 µg/mL), PGT121 (23 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.1 µg/mL), 354BG18 (19 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.06 µg/mL) and PGT128 (22 isolates with a mean IC50 of 0.04 µg/mL).
evidence: This is based on comparison of neutralization data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mean IC50 of Ab1485 against 14 pseudoviruses is identical to the mean IC50 of PGT121, 0.06 µg/mL.
source: The mean IC50 of Ab1485 against the 14 pseudoviruses for which there is available neutralization data for all these human bNAbs is identical to the mean IC50 of PGT121, 0.06 µg/mL, and significantly lower than the mean IC50 of PGT13, 17.5 µg/mL.
evidence: This is based on analysis of neutralization data.

claim: The mean IC50 of Ab1485 against 14 pseudoviruses is significantly lower than the mean IC50 of PGT13, 17.5 µg/mL.
source: The mean IC50 of Ab1485 against the 14 pseudoviruses for which there is available neutralization data for all these human bNAbs is identical to the mean IC50 of PGT121, 0.06 µg/mL, and significantly lower than the mean IC50 of PGT13, 17.5 µg/mL.
evidence: This is based on analysis of neutralization data.

claim: Ab1485 is a potent neutralizer with limited breadth compared to some of the human bNAbs reported to date.
source: We conclude that Ab1485 is a potent neutralizer with limited breadth compared to some of the human bNAbs reported to date (Sok and Burton, 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neutralization data and supported by citation.

claim: Ab1485 combines the germline V-gene segments VH4_2M and VL124_30.
source: Ab1485 combines the germline V-gene segments VH4_2M and VL124_30 and is highly mutated (33 and 25 nucleotide mutations in the VH and VL genes respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ab1485 is highly mutated with 33 and 25 nucleotide mutations in the VH and VL genes respectively.
source: Ab1485 combines the germline V-gene segments VH4_2M and VL124_30 and is highly mutated (33 and 25 nucleotide mutations in the VH and VL genes respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Ab1485 has a 20-residue CDRH3.
source: It has a 20-residue CDRH3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No other family members of Ab1485 were found when analyzing the LN biopsy collected from macaque CE8J at week 115 after SHIVAD8 challenge.
source: We did not find any other family members of Ab1485 when analyzing the LN biopsy collected from macaque CE8J at the time of necropsy (week 115 after SHIVAD8 challenge).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the clonal analysis.

claim: The binding of Ab1485 to BG505 was inhibited by the V3-glycan bNAb 10–1074.
source: The binding of Ab1485 to BG505 was inhibited by the V3-glycan bNAb 10–1074 but not by any of the other human bNAbs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The binding of Ab1485 to BG505 was not inhibited by 3BNC117, 8ANC195, PG9, or VRC34.
source: The binding of Ab1485 to BG505 was inhibited by the V3-glycan bNAb 10–1074 but not by any of the other human bNAbs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The neutralizing activity of Ab1485 was dependent on the potential N-linked glycosylation sites at N332gp120 and N156gp120.
source: The neutralizing activity of Ab1485 was dependent on the potential N-linked glycosylation sites at N332gp120 and N156gp120, but unaffected by mutations that interfere with the binding of human bNAbs to the interface (N611D), the CD4-binding site (T278A+ A281T), the V1V2 apex (N160K), the MPER (F673L) or the fusion peptide (N88Q) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The neutralizing activity of Ab1485 was unaffected by mutations that interfere with the binding of human bNAbs to the interface, the CD4-binding site, the V1V2 apex, the MPER or the fusion peptide.
source: The neutralizing activity of Ab1485 was dependent on the potential N-linked glycosylation sites at N332gp120 and N156gp120, but unaffected by mutations that interfere with the binding of human bNAbs to the interface (N611D), the CD4-binding site (T278A+ A281T), the V1V2 apex (N160K), the MPER (F673L) or the fusion peptide (N88Q) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The competition ELISA and neutralization results suggested that Ab1485 targets the V3-glycan patch in Env.
source: In conclusion, the competition ELISA and neutralization results suggested that Ab1485 targets the V3-glycan patch in Env.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the competition and neutralization data.

claim: A 3.5 Å cryo-EM structure of Ab1485 in complex with the BG505 SOSIP.664 trimer and 8ANC195 was determined.
source: To elucidate the molecular details of Env recognition by Ab1485, we determined a 3.5 Å cryo-EM structure of Ab1485 in complex with the BG505 SOSIP.664 trimer and the gp120-gp41 interface targeting antibody, 8ANC195 (Scharf et al., 2014; Scharf et al., 2015; Figure 3A, Figure 1—source data 1-table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The structure of the Ab1485-Env complex revealed recognition of an epitope focused on the N332gp120 glycan, the gp120 GDIR peptide motif, and V1 loop.
source: The structure of the Ab1485-Env complex revealed recognition of an epitope focused on the N332gp120 glycan, the gp120 GDIR peptide motif, and V1 loop (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ab1485's primary interaction was with the N332gp120 glycan (Man6GlcNAc2), which interfaces almost entirely with the CDRH3 loop.
source: In common with human-derived V3/N332gp120 glycan-targeting bNAbs, Ab1485's primary interaction was with the N332gp120 glycan (Man6GlcNAc2), which interfaces almost entirely with the CDRH3 loop (Figure 3C) (~400 Å2 antibody buried surface area (BSA)).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ab1485 makes secondary contacts with the N156gp120 glycan (~275 Å2 antibody BSA).
source: In addition to the N332gp120 glycan, Ab1485 makes secondary contacts with the N156gp120 glycan (~275 Å2 antibody BSA), which frames Ab1485's VH domain at the gp120 V3 epitope, rationalizing the observed loss in neutralization activity when tested against the JRCSF ∆N156gp120 glycan virus (Figure 2C) and consistent with faster dissociation kinetics observed in surface plasmon resonance (SPR) binding experiments that demonstrated a faster dissociation rate for a SOSIP that lacks the N156gp120 glycan (RC1) compared to a SOSIP that contains the N156gp120 potential N-linked glycosylation site (BG505) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by structural data and SPR experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Ab1485 adopts a Env-binding orientation most closely related to PGT128.
source: When compared to the poses of human-derived bNAbs (Figure 3D–F) and V3-targeting antibodies elicited in rabbits or rhesus macaques by vaccination or SHIVBG505 challenge (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), Ab1485 adopts a Env-binding orientation in a manner most closely related to PGT128, which primarily uses its heavy chain to interact with the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope (Kong et al., 2015; Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Ab1485 lacks any V-gene insertions or deletions.
source: However, in contrast to PGT128, Ab1485 lacks any V-gene insertions or deletions and its orientation is rotated ~90° relative to PGT128, resulting in a unique Env-binding orientation that shifts interactions away from the N301gp120 N-glycan and towards the N156gp120 glycan, and moves the light chain outside of the underlying V3-epitope (Figure 3 and Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4A–C.

claim: Ab1485's orientation is rotated ~90° relative to PGT128.
source: However, in contrast to PGT128, Ab1485 lacks any V-gene insertions or deletions and its orientation is rotated ~90° relative to PGT128, resulting in a unique Env-binding orientation that shifts interactions away from the N301gp120 N-glycan and towards the N156gp120 glycan, and moves the light chain outside of the underlying V3-epitope (Figure 3 and Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4A–C.

claim: Interactions with the N-linked glycans and gp120 peptide components are almost exclusively mediated by the Ab1485 heavy chain.
source: Thus, interactions with the N-linked glycans and gp120 peptide components are almost exclusively mediated by the Ab1485 heavy chain (Figure 4A,B; 1255 Å2 vs 65 Å2 buried surface areas for HC and LC components of Ab1485 paratope, respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Ab1485 may not be restricted by light chain pairing or require the consensus light chain sequence motifs commonly observed in human-derived V3/N332gp120-glycan-targeting bNAbs.
source: This observation suggests that Ab1485 may not be restricted by light chain pairing or require the consensus light chain sequence motifs commonly observed in human-derived V3/N332gp120-glycan-targeting bNAbs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation that the heavy chain dominates the interaction.

claim: All three heavy chain CDR loops of Ab1485 contact the 324GDIR327 gp120 peptide motif at the base of the V3-loop.
source: Closer examination of the Ab1485 epitope revealed that all three heavy chain CDR loops contact the 324GDIR327 gp120 peptide motif at the base of the V3-loop, which contrasts interactions by both heavy and light chain CDR loops observed in 10–1074/PGT121-like and BG18 bNAbs (Gristick et al., 2016; Barnes et al., 2018; Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: The primary molecular contacts of Ab1485 with the GDIR motif are with CDRH1 residues R30HC, S31HC, and N32HC.
source: The primary molecular contacts are with CDRH1 residues R30HC, S31HC, and N32HC, which form potential hydrogen bonds with backbone and sidechain atoms from residues G324gp120 and D325gp120 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CDRH1 residues of Ab1485 mimic interactions made by CDRL1/L3 residues in PGT121/101074-like bNAbs with Env.
source: Interestingly, these CDRH1 residues mimic interactions made by CDRL1/L3 residues in PGT121/101074-like bNAbs with Env, providing evidence for a convergent chemical mechanism of interactions with the gp120 GDIR motif, as previously shown for BG18 (Barnes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and supported by citation.

claim: Ab1485 residue R30HC forms secondary interactions with V1 loop residues V134gp120 and T135gp120.
source: Moreover, Ab1485 residue R30HC forms secondary interactions with V1 loop residues V134gp120 and T135gp120, resembling similar arginine-gp120 V1-loop interactions observed in 10–1074, BG18, and PGT128 (Kong et al., 2015; Gristick et al., 2016; Barnes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and supported by citations.

claim: The Ab1485-BG505 structure reveals an alternate binding mode involving cation-pi stacking interactions between R327gp120 and W99HC.
source: The Ab1485-BG505 structure reveals an alternate binding mode that involves the guanidinium moiety of R327gp120 forming cation-pi stacking interactions with W99HC at the tip of the Ab1485's CDRH3, while also participating in hydrogen bonding with the backbone carbonyl group (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Salt-bridge formation between R327gp120 and an acidic CDRH3 residue found in V3-targeting bNAbs may not be as critical to targeting the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope.
source: This observation suggests that salt-bridge formation between R327gp120 and an acidic CDRH3 residue found in V3-targeting bNAbs may not be as critical to targeting the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: Ab1485 was not polyreactive.
source: Ab1485 was not polyreactive, as shown by ELISAs against a series of antigens (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and Ab1485-LS had a half-life of 2.67 days in transgenic human FcRn mice (Roopenian et al., 2003; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ab1485-LS had a half-life of 2.67 days in transgenic human FcRn mice.
source: Ab1485 was not polyreactive, as shown by ELISAs against a series of antigens (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and Ab1485-LS had a half-life of 2.67 days in transgenic human FcRn mice (Roopenian et al., 2003; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Four macaques receiving Ab1485 remained uninfected throughout a 25-week observation period after high dose SHIVAD8 challenge.
source: Two historical control monkeys (Yamamoto, 2015) receiving no mAb, rapidly became infected, generating peak levels of plasma viremia on day 14 post-challenge. In contrast, the four macaques receiving Ab1485 remained uninfected throughout a 25-week observation period (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Two historical control monkeys receiving no mAb rapidly became infected, generating peak levels of plasma viremia on day 14 post-challenge.
source: Two historical control monkeys (Yamamoto, 2015) receiving no mAb, rapidly became infected, generating peak levels of plasma viremia on day 14 post-challenge. In contrast, the four macaques receiving Ab1485 remained uninfected throughout a 25-week observation period (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B and supported by citation.

claim: Neutralizing antibody titers persisted in the peripheral blood for at least 50 days after the virus challenge.
source: Neutralizing antibody titers persisted in the peripheral blood for at least 50 days after the virus challenge (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ab1485-macaque-LS protects macaques from high dose intrarectal SHIVAD8 infection.
source: We conclude that Ab1485-macaque-LS protects macaques from high dose intrarectal SHIVAD8 infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the protection data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Indian-origin rhesus macaques infected with SHIV are an important model for evaluating HIV-1 prevention and therapy strategies.
source: Indian-origin rhesus macaques infected with SHIV are an important model for evaluating HIV-1 prevention and therapy strategies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Monoclonal Ab1485 obtained from single-B-cells purified on the basis of HIV-1 Env-binding by cell sorting neutralized 16 of 42 of the HIV-1 strains tested with IC50 lower than 1 µg.ml.
source: Monoclonal Ab1485 obtained from single-B-cells purified on the basis of HIV-1 Env-binding by cell sorting neutralized 16 of 42 of the HIV-1 strains tested with IC50 lower than 1 µg.ml.
evidence: This is based on the neutralization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rhesus macaques develop anti-HIV-1 V3-glycan patch bNAbs that resemble human bNAbs.
source: Thus, rhesus macaques develop anti-HIV-1 V3-glycan patch bNAbs that resemble human bNAbs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the combined data.

claim: 10–20% of HIV-1 infected humans develop antibodies that can neutralize a number of different HIV-1 strains.
source: As many as 10–20% of HIV-1 infected humans develop antibodies that can neutralize a number of different HIV-1 strains, but only an elite few (1–2%) produce potent broadly neutralizing serologic activity (Landais and Moore, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Landais and Moore, 2018.

claim: Only 1–2% of HIV-1 infected humans produce potent broadly neutralizing serologic activity.
source: As many as 10–20% of HIV-1 infected humans develop antibodies that can neutralize a number of different HIV-1 strains, but only an elite few (1–2%) produce potent broadly neutralizing serologic activity (Landais and Moore, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Landais and Moore, 2018.

claim: Elite humoral responders typically take 1–3 years to produce bNAbs.
source: The elite humoral responders typically take 1–3 years to produce bNAbs, which is highly unusual for an antibody response.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Human bNAbs carry large numbers of somatic mutations that are required for their neutralizing activity.
source: Single cell antibody cloning revealed that human bNAbs carry large numbers of somatic mutations that are required for their neutralizing activity (Mouquet et al., 2012; Scheid et al., 2011; Scheid et al., 2009; Xiao et al., 2009; Muster et al., 1993; Zhou et al., 2010; Hoot et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2013; Sok et al., 2013; Kepler et al., 2014; Bonsignori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The development of bNAbs required a prolonged series of sequential interactions between the antibody-producing B lymphocytes and virus escape variants to drive antibody maturation.
source: This observation led to the proposal that the development of bNAbs required a prolonged series of sequential interactions between the antibody-producing B lymphocytes and virus escape variants to drive antibody maturation (Scheid et al., 2009; Dimitrov, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Prospective studies of virus and antibody evolution supported the concept that bNAb development requires sequential interactions between B cells and virus escape variants.
source: Elegant prospective studies of virus and antibody evolution supported this concept (Liao et al., 2013; Bonsignori et al., 2017; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2012; Bhiman et al., 2015), and sequential immunization experiments reproduced it in knock in mice (Escolano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sequential immunization experiments reproduced bNAb development in knock in mice.
source: Elegant prospective studies of virus and antibody evolution supported this concept (Liao et al., 2013; Bonsignori et al., 2017; Doria-Rose et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2012; Bhiman et al., 2015), and sequential immunization experiments reproduced it in knock in mice (Escolano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Escolano et al., 2016.

claim: Monoclonal antibody Ab1485 resembles human bNAbs in high levels of somatic mutation.
source: Monoclonal antibody Ab1485 resembles human bNAbs in many important respects including the high levels of somatic mutation suggesting a requirement for sequential interaction between B cells and the virus to drive bNAb evolution in macaques.
evidence: This is based on the sequence analysis data presented earlier.

claim: Ab1485 suggests a requirement for sequential interaction between B cells and the virus to drive bNAb evolution in macaques.

evidence: This is an inference based on the high mutation levels observed.

claim: Infection with SHIVs bearing the Envs of transmitted founder (T/F) HIV-1 viruses that induced bNAbs in humans recapitulates key events of the interplay between HIV-1 and antibodies in the infected individuals.
source: This process of virus and antibody co-evolution has been recently shown in macaques in a study by Roark and colleagues (preprint in bioRxiv, Roark et al., 2020). Their work shows that infection with SHIVs bearing the Envs of transmitted founder (T/F) HIV-1 viruses that induced bNAbs in humans, recapitulates key events of the previously reported interplay between HIV-1 and antibodies in the infected individuals.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roark et al., 2020.

claim: Infection with SHIV.CH505 induced the development of a lineage of V2-apex bNAbs that shows certain breadth and potency against tier 1 and tier two pseudoviruses.
source: Infection with one of these T/F-SHIVs, SHIV.CH505, induced the development of a lineage of V2-apex bNAbs that shows certain breadth and potency against tier 1 and tier two pseudoviruses.
evidence: This is based on the cited work by Roark et al., 2020.

claim: RHA1.V2.01 has comparable frequencies of IgH V(D)J nucleotide mutations to Ab1485 (8.5% in RHA1.V2.01 vs 8.6% in Ab1485).
source: The most mutated member of this lineage, RHA1.V2.01, has comparable frequencies of IgH V(D)J nucleotide mutations to Ab1485 (8.5% in RHA1.V2.01 vs 8.6% in Ab1485) and slightly lower mutation frequencies in the IgL (6.2% in RHA1.V2.01 vs 7.55% in Ab1485).
evidence: This is a comparison based on data from the cited work and the current study.

claim: RHA1.V2.01 has slightly lower mutation frequencies in the IgL than Ab1485 (6.2% in RHA1.V2.01 vs 7.55% in Ab1485).
source: The most mutated member of this lineage, RHA1.V2.01, has comparable frequencies of IgH V(D)J nucleotide mutations to Ab1485 (8.5% in RHA1.V2.01 vs 8.6% in Ab1485) and slightly lower mutation frequencies in the IgL (6.2% in RHA1.V2.01 vs 7.55% in Ab1485).
evidence: This is a comparison based on data from the cited work and the current study.

claim: RHA1.V2.01 and Ab1485 show similar breadth when considering isolates neutralized at IC50 <1 µg/mL (30.7% for RHA1.V2.01 vs 38.1% for Ab1485).
source: Regarding the neutralization activity, RHA1.V2.01 and Ab1485 show similar breadth when considering isolates neutralized at IC50 <1 µg/mL (30.7% for RHA1.V2.01 vs 38.1% for Ab1485) but Ab1485 is more potent against the reported neutralized isolates (mean IC50 of RHA1.V2.01 = 0.214 µg/mL vs mean IC50 of Ab1485 0.055 µg/mL).
evidence: This is a comparison based on neutralization data.

claim: Ab1485 is more potent than RHA1.V2.01 against the reported neutralized isolates (mean IC50 of RHA1.V2.01 = 0.214 µg/mL vs mean IC50 of Ab1485 0.055 µg/mL).
source: Regarding the neutralization activity, RHA1.V2.01 and Ab1485 show similar breadth when considering isolates neutralized at IC50 <1 µg/mL (30.7% for RHA1.V2.01 vs 38.1% for Ab1485) but Ab1485 is more potent against the reported neutralized isolates (mean IC50 of RHA1.V2.01 = 0.214 µg/mL vs mean IC50 of Ab1485 0.055 µg/mL).
evidence: This is a comparison based on neutralization data.

claim: Ab1485 resembles PGT128 in that most of the interactions with the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope are mediated by heavy chain CDR loops.
source: Monoclonal antibody Ab1485 targets the glycan patch that surrounds the conserved GDIR peptide at the base of the V3 loop, an epitope that is frequently targeted by human bNAbs. Ab1485 resembles PGT128 in that most of the interactions with the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope are mediated by heavy chain CDR loops, including conserved interactions with the N332gp120 glycan and gp120 GDIR peptide motif.
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

source: Recent studies in macaques showed that after priming with a designed immunogen that focuses the response to the V3-glycan epitope, antibodies with binding features of V3-glycan-targeting bNAbs can be isolated (Escolano et al., 2019).

claim: Structural analysis of 1485 provides evidence that effective bNAbs targeting the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope are not restricted to PGT128, BG18 or 10–1074/PGT121-like binding mechanisms.
source: Overall, structural analysis of 1485 provides: (i) evidence that effective bNAbs targeting the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope are not restricted to PGT128, BG18 or 10–1074/PGT121-like binding mechanisms, (ii) critical structural insights towards immunogen design efforts to elicit neutralizing antibodies, including alternative binding modes that do not include light chain interactions, and (iii) evidence that SHIVAD8-infected macaques are capable of generating bNAbs that target the V3/N332gp120-glycan epitope in a manner similar to human-derived bNAbs, and therefore represent an excellent animal model for developing HIV-1 vaccines targeting this site.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.
